alt: Integer solutions of 3x+5y=1. The hollow point (1,-2/5) lies on the real line but is not an integer solution. The filled points (2,-1), (-3,2) and (7,-4) differ by (5,-3). A real line contains infinitely many real points; arithmetic asks which of them land on the integer lattice.

Euclid’s algorithm cuts the largest possible squares from an a\times b rectangle; the number of squares of each size is the quotient q_k, and the last square has side \gcd(a,b). On the left, 34\times21: every quotient except the last is 1 (the last is 2), the square sizes are Fibonacci numbers, and the algorithm is as slow as possible (Theorem 1.8). On the right, 45\times16: large quotients, few steps.
Portrait of Pafnuty Chebyshev (1821–1894).

The sieve up to 50. A cross marks a multiple of 2 greater than 2; a slash marks a still unremoved multiple of 3; a small square marks 25 and 35, removed at the 5-stage; a diamond marks 49, removed at the 7-stage. Unmarked entries are primes. Shapes distinguish the stages even in a black-and-white paperback.

Left: the staircase \pi(x) for x\le100 against \frac x{\ln x} and the logarithmic integral \mathrm{Li}(x)=\int_2^x\frac{\mathrm dt}{\ln t}. Right: the ratios \pi(x)\big/\frac x{\ln x} and \pi(x)/\mathrm{Li}(x) up to x=10^5. At 10^5 the first is still 1.104, while the second is already 0.996: \mathrm{Li}(x) is by far the better approximation.

Left: x\mapsto(x\bmod3,x\bmod4) for x=0,\dots,11. Each step x\to x+1 moves diagonally (the arrows show the steps that do not wrap around), and every cell is hit exactly once. Right: with the non-coprime moduli 2 and 4, the walk closes up after \operatorname{lcm}(2,4)=4 steps, so half the cells (grey) are never reached and the others are hit twice.

Two simple roots of X^2+1 lifting through powers of 5. The integers at each level are representatives, not increasing real approximations: 57 and 68 both square to -1 modulo 125. Each arrow records reduction modulo the preceding power of 5.

Orders of units modulo 13. For each divisor d of 12, the bar height is N(d)=\varphi(d): 1,1,2,2,2,4. The twelve units are partitioned by their exact orders; merely knowing x^d=1 counts units whose order divides d, which is a different question. The rightmost bar gives the four primitive roots.

The twelve units modulo 13, placed in the order 2^0,2^1,\dots,2^{11}. Left: multiplying by the primitive root 2 moves one step and visits every unit. Right: 3=2^4, so multiplying by 3 jumps four steps, and the units split into four cycles of length \operatorname{ord}_{13}(3)=3. The shaded units 2,6,11,7 are the \varphi(12)=4 primitive roots, the powers 2^j with \gcd(j,12)=1.
Portrait of Carl Friedrich Gauss (1777–1855).

Each cell records \left(\frac pq\right): row prime p, column prime q. A plus means a non-zero square, a minus a non-square, and 0 on the diagonal records divisibility. Compare cells reflected across the diagonal: they disagree exactly when both primes are 3 modulo 4. Signs carry the information even in black-and-white print.

Eisenstein’s count for p=7 and q=11. The 3\times5=15 lattice points of the rectangle are split by the diagonal y=\frac{11}7x, which passes through none of them, into T(11,7)=8 and T(7,11)=7. So \left(\frac{11}7\right)\left(\frac7{11}\right)=(-1)^{15}=-1: indeed 11\equiv2^2 is a square modulo 7, but 7 is not a square modulo 11.

An orchard in the square 1\le a,b\le12. Filled circles are the 91 visible trees, those with \gcd(a,b)=1; crosses are hidden trees. On the dashed ray through (2,3), the trees (4,6), (6,9) and (8,12) stand behind it. Visibility is decided by the first lattice point on each ray. The finite fraction 91/144 is about 0.632, not yet the limiting 6/\pi^2.

Every divisor of 72 occupies exactly one cell, labelled 2^i3^j. There are 4\cdot3 cells. Summing the rows factors the total as (1+2+4+8)(1+3+9)=195. A product over primes is a compressed record of independent exponent choices.

The 111 lattice points with ab\le30, so \sum_{n\le30}\tau(n)=111. Dirichlet counts the points with a\le\sqrt{30} (blue and green) and, by symmetry, those with b\le\sqrt{30} (blue and orange). The blue square is then counted twice, so it is subtracted once: 2\sum_{a\le5}\lfloor30/a\rfloor-5^2=2\cdot68-25=111. Only \sqrt x columns are summed, which shrinks the error from O(x) to O(\sqrt x).
Portrait of Pierre de Fermat (1601–1665).

The first quadrant of x^2+y^2=65. Its integer points are (1,8), (4,7), (7,4) and (8,1); reflecting them across the axes gives 16 representations when signs and order count. None lies on an axis, so each reflection creates a new point.

The N(6)=113 lattice points in the disc of radius 6, against 36\pi\approx113.1. Each point (x,y) owns the unit square [x,x+1[\times[y,y+1[. The squares cover the disc of radius R-\sqrt2 and stay inside the disc of radius R+\sqrt2 (dashed), which squeezes N(R) between the two areas.

Approximation as a lattice problem. A point (q,p) represents p/q; its vertical distance from p=\sqrt2\,q is |q\sqrt2-p|, while its slope error is |\sqrt2-p/q|. The labelled convergents alternate below and above the line. Distances, rather than colours, tell the story.

How good are the convergents? For \varphi and \sqrt2, whose partial quotients are constant, q_n^2\left|x-\frac{p_n}{q_n}\right| settles at \frac1{\sqrt5}\approx0.447 and \frac1{2\sqrt2}\approx0.354. For \pi, the dip at n=3 is \frac{355}{113}, followed by the huge partial quotient 292: 113^2\left|\pi-\frac{355}{113}\right|\approx0.0034. For e, every third value dips, following the pattern 1,2k,1 of its partial quotients.

The 3–4–5 triangle has area 6, semiperimeter 6, and inradius 1. The three dashed radii meet the sides at right angles. The formula r=(a+b-c)/2 connects the geometry with the integer parameters of a Pythagorean triple.

Left: the chord method on the unit circle. Each line through (-1,0) with rational slope t meets the circle again at a rational point, and every rational point arises this way; t=\frac12 gives the triple (3,4,5), t=\frac23 gives (5,12,13). Right: the first levels of the tree of Markov triples (Theorem 9.6). Each triple (a,b,c) with c largest has two children, (a,c,3ac-b) and (b,c,3bc-a).

Division in \mathbb{Z}[i]. The cross is a/b=7/13-(17/13)i; the circled lattice point is the rounded quotient q=1-i. Their distance is \sqrt{4/13}<1. The dashed square is the rounding cell of q; its farthest corners are at distance 1/\sqrt2.

The irreducibles of norm at most 225 in \mathbb{Z}[i] (left) and \mathbb{Z}[\omega] (right). Blue: the factors \pi of a prime p=\pi\bar\pi with p\equiv1\pmod4 (left) or p\equiv1\pmod3 (right). Red: the primes q\equiv3\pmod4 (left) or q\equiv2\pmod3 (right), which stay irreducible, with their associates. Green: the associates of 1+i and of 1-\omega, whose squares are 2 and 3 up to units.

The units x+y\sqrt2 of \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2] with x,y\ge0 lie on the two hyperbolas x^2-2y^2=\pm1, alternately. Multiplication by \varepsilon=1+\sqrt2 is the linear map (x,y)\mapsto(x+2y,x+y), which preserves the pair of hyperbolas and jumps from each unit to the next.

\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}] is a lattice in \mathbb{C}, and an ideal is a sublattice stable under multiplication by \sqrt{-5}. The ideal P (blue) contains every second point, the ideal (2)=P^2 (circled) every fourth. P is a perfectly good “number”, it just is not the set of multiples of any one element.

Four coefficient remainders modulo (2) merge into two remainders modulo P=(2,1+\sqrt{-5}). Adding 1+\sqrt{-5} pairs the two solid dots and pairs the two open dots. Passing to the larger ideal identifies more points.
Portrait of Hermann Minkowski (1864–1909).
How the primes p<240 factor in \mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}], computed with Theorem 12.7 and Exercise [ex:fermat5].

The 2-adic integers as an infinite binary tree. A node at depth k is a residue class modulo 2^k (a ball of radius 2^{-k}), and an infinite path from the root is a 2-adic integer, read off as its binary digits. The dashed path, all digits 1, is -1; the solid path that branches from it is \frac13=1+2+0\cdot4+8+0\cdot16+\cdots.
|n|_2 for 1\le n\le 64: the “ruler function”. Most integers have 2-adic size 1; the multiples of high powers of 2 are the small ones.

The root of X^2+1 congruent to 2 modulo 5. At each level, only one of the five candidate lifts survives; the solid path records 2,7,57,182. Dashed branches show the four rejected choices at each step.
